title: 2 Kings 21:1–18
context: Manasseh reverses Hezekiah’s reforms, filling the temple with idolatry, sacrificing his son, and shedding much innocent blood. The LORD announces through the prophets that Jerusalem will be judged like Samaria. Kings records no repentance; 2 Chronicles 33 gives a fuller account that readers weigh alongside this one.

verses.text: Manasseh was twelve years old when he began to reign, and he reigned fifty-five years in Jerusalem. His mother’s name was Hephzibah.
verses.arminianNotes: Manasseh begins to reign at twelve and reigns fifty-five years. Arminian readers note that the longest reign in Judah’s history becomes one of its most destructive, showing how much harm a leader’s chosen path can do over time.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the length of the reign as part of the narrator’s sober framing. A long reign is not presented as a sign of divine approval, and God’s patience during it does not mean indifference to evil.

verses.text: He did that which was evil in the LORD’s sight, after the abominations of the nations whom the LORD cast out before the children of Israel.
verses.arminianNotes: Manasseh “did that which was evil in the LORD’s sight, after the abominations of the nations.” Arminian readers see a king who knowingly turned Judah toward the practices God had judged in Canaan.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the narrator’s verdict tying Manasseh to the nations driven out before Israel. The comparison prepares for the later judgment, since Judah now repeats what brought judgment on others.

verses.text: For he built again the high places which Hezekiah his father had destroyed; and he raised up altars for Baal, and made an Asherah, as Ahab king of Israel did, and worshiped all the army of the sky, and served them.
verses.arminianNotes: He rebuilds the high places Hezekiah destroyed, raises altars for Baal, makes an Asherah “as Ahab king of Israel did,” and worships the army of the sky. Arminian readers see a deliberate reversal of his father’s reforms.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see Manasseh undoing Hezekiah’s faithfulness. The comparison with Ahab links Judah’s king with the most notorious king of the north, showing how far Judah has fallen.

verses.text: He built altars in the LORD’s house, of which the LORD said, “I will put my name in Jerusalem.”
verses.arminianNotes: He builds altars in the LORD’s house, of which the LORD said, “I will put my name in Jerusalem.” Arminian readers see sacrilege in the very place God had chosen for his name.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the temple itself defiled. The narrator sets Manasseh’s altars beside God’s promise, highlighting the gravity of corrupting the place devoted to the LORD’s name.

verses.text: He built altars for all the army of the sky in the two courts of the LORD’s house.
verses.arminianNotes: He builds altars for the army of the sky in both temple courts. Arminian readers see idolatry spreading through the sanctuary, leaving no space reserved for the worship of the LORD alone.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the thoroughness of Manasseh’s apostasy. Star worship in the courts of the LORD’s house shows the extent to which Judah’s worship had been corrupted.

verses.text: He made his son to pass through the fire, practiced sorcery, used enchantments, and dealt with those who had familiar spirits and with wizards. He did much evil in the LORD’s sight, to provoke him to anger.
verses.arminianNotes: Manasseh “made his son to pass through the fire,” practiced sorcery, and consulted mediums. Arminian readers name this plainly as child sacrifice, forbidden in Deuteronomy 18:10, and grieve the life of a child given to idolatry.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise grieve this sacrifice of a child as a grave evil, done “to provoke him to anger.” Readers in this tradition stress that the narrator records it soberly, without detail, to show the depth of the king’s rebellion.

verses.text: He set the engraved image of Asherah that he had made in the house of which the LORD said to David and to Solomon his son, “In this house, and in Jerusalem, which I have chosen out of all the tribes of Israel, I will put my name forever;
verses.arminianNotes: He sets the Asherah image in the house of which the LORD said, “In this house, and in Jerusalem … I will put my name forever.” Arminian readers see the idol placed where God’s name was meant to dwell.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the image set against God’s promise to David and Solomon, recorded in 1 Kings 9:3. The contrast between God’s chosen house and Manasseh’s idol is stark.

verses.text: I will not cause the feet of Israel to wander any more out of the land which I gave their fathers, if only they will observe to do according to all that I have commanded them, and according to all the law that my servant Moses commanded them.”
verses.arminianNotes: God had said, “I will not cause the feet of Israel to wander any more … if only they will observe to do according to all that I have commanded them.” Arminian readers see the conditional nature of secure dwelling in the land.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the condition attached to the promise of the land. Readers in this tradition generally hold that God’s covenant faithfulness is not undone by this condition, while Judah’s disobedience brings real consequences.

verses.text: But they didn’t listen, and Manasseh seduced them to do that which is evil more than the nations did whom the LORD destroyed before the children of Israel.
verses.arminianNotes: “But they didn’t listen, and Manasseh seduced them to do that which is evil more than the nations did.” Arminian readers see both the people and their king responsible for refusing God’s word.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the king leading the people astray and the people following. The verdict that Judah did worse than the nations shows how deep the corruption ran.

verses.text: The LORD spoke by his servants the prophets, saying,
verses.arminianNotes: “The LORD spoke by his servants the prophets.” Arminian readers see God continuing to warn Judah through his messengers, giving opportunity to turn even in a dark time.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see God sending his word through the prophets. The verse shows that judgment did not come without warning, though the prophets are not named here.

verses.text: “Because Manasseh king of Judah has done these abominations, and has done wickedly above all that the Amorites did, who were before him, and has also made Judah to sin with his idols;
verses.arminianNotes: The prophets say Manasseh “has done wickedly above all that the Amorites did … and has also made Judah to sin with his idols.” Arminian readers see the king held responsible for leading the nation into sin.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see Manasseh’s guilt measured against the Amorites. The charge emphasizes both his personal wickedness and his influence over the people.

verses.text: therefore the LORD the God of Israel says, ‘Behold, I will bring such evil on Jerusalem and Judah that whoever hears of it, both his ears will tingle.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says, “I will bring such evil on Jerusalem and Judah that whoever hears of it, both his ears will tingle.” Arminian readers see a solemn warning of coming disaster.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see God announcing judgment of shocking severity. The image of tingling ears conveys how startling the coming catastrophe will be to all who hear of it.

verses.text: I will stretch over Jerusalem the line of Samaria, and the plumb line of Ahab’s house; and I will wipe Jerusalem as a man wipes a dish, wiping it and turning it upside down.
verses.arminianNotes: “I will stretch over Jerusalem the line of Samaria … I will wipe Jerusalem as a man wipes a dish.” Arminian readers see Jerusalem measured by the same standard as the fallen north.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see God applying the same judgment to Judah as to Samaria. The image of wiping a dish and turning it upside down conveys a thorough clearing out.

verses.text: I will cast off the remnant of my inheritance and deliver them into the hands of their enemies. They will become a prey and a plunder to all their enemies,
verses.arminianNotes: “I will cast off the remnant of my inheritance and deliver them into the hands of their enemies.” Arminian readers see the painful consequence of persistent covenant unfaithfulness.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see God’s judgment on his own inheritance. Readers in this tradition note that later prophetic promises of restoration show God’s purposes for his people did not end with exile.

verses.text: because they have done that which is evil in my sight, and have provoked me to anger since the day their fathers came out of Egypt, even to this day.’ ”
verses.arminianNotes: “… because they have done that which is evil in my sight, and have provoked me to anger since the day their fathers came out of Egypt.” Arminian readers see judgment as the outcome of a long history of rebellion.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see God’s patience spanning generations before judgment. The verse frames Manasseh’s sin as the climax of a long pattern rather than an isolated failure.

verses.text: Moreover Manasseh shed innocent blood very much, until he had filled Jerusalem from one end to another; in addition to his sin with which he made Judah to sin, in doing that which was evil in the LORD’s sight.
verses.arminianNotes: “Manasseh shed innocent blood very much, until he had filled Jerusalem from one end to another.” Arminian readers grieve the loss of innocent lives under a king who abused his power.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise name this violence plainly and soberly. 2 Kings 24:3–4 later cites this innocent blood as part of the reason for Judah’s fall, showing how seriously God regards it.

verses.text: Now the rest of the acts of Manasseh, and all that he did, and his sin that he sinned, aren’t they written in the book of the chronicles of the kings of Judah?
verses.arminianNotes: The rest of Manasseh’s acts are written “in the book of the chronicles of the kings of Judah.” Arminian readers see the narrator pointing to fuller records while focusing on the king’s spiritual legacy.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the selective focus of the account. 2 Chronicles 33:10–17 records a later humbling of Manasseh, and interpreters in this tradition discuss how that account relates to the verdict in Kings.

verses.text: Manasseh slept with his fathers, and was buried in the garden of his own house, in the garden of Uzza; and Amon his son reigned in his place.
verses.arminianNotes: Manasseh dies and is buried in the garden of Uzza, and Amon reigns. Arminian readers note that he is buried in the garden of his own house, a detail the narrator records without explaining the reason for it.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise note the burial location without assigning a reason. The narrator simply records Manasseh’s death and his son’s succession.
